questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Octave equivalence
questions.learningObjective: Identify why two pitches an octave apart share a pitch class
questions.stem: Mara's speaker spec sheet lists 220 Hz and 440 Hz as the same tone class for octave labelling. Which statement best explains why the brief can treat them as equivalent?

options.text: The two pitches are one octave apart, so they share a pitch class and sound the same.
Frequencies double, but the ear groups anything above 1000 Hz into a single timbre class.
options.misconception: Believes the ear ignores pitch above 1000 Hz

options.text: Both notes carry the same letter name, and letter names are what define equivalence.
options.misconception: Believes letter names, not pitch class, create equivalence

options.text: Doubling the frequency always produces a brighter timbre, so the two notes differ.
options.misconception: Believes doubling frequency breaks the equivalence

questions.explanation: An octave spans twelve semitones and twelve pitch classes, so 220 Hz and 440 Hz share a pitch class. Doubling frequency changes timbre, not pitch class, so the two are equivalent.
questions.hint: Twelve semitones per octave.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval pattern of a major scale
questions.learningObjective: Explain where the half steps fall in a major scale
questions.stem: In an engineer's brief, the firmware builds a major scale from a root note and asks the reviewer to justify the pattern of steps. Explain why a major scale places half steps exactly where it does.

answer.exemplar: A major scale runs to its own octave using the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The half steps fall between the third and fourth degrees and between the seventh and the octave, which is what gives the major third and the major seventh their sizes and lets the leading tone sit a semitone below the tonic.

questions.explanation: The whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half pattern is the definition of the major scale. Half steps at degrees three to four and seven to eight create the major third and the leading tone.
questions.hint: Look at where the semitone pairs fall.

questions.stem: A tuning-table log records the semitone offsets used by the prototype: step sizes of 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 semitones between successive scale degrees. Which tuning system produces these step sizes?

options.text: Twelve-tone equal temperament, where every semitone is identical in size.
Just intonation, where ratios such as five to four replace equal semitone steps.
options.misconception: Believes equal-sized steps come from just intonation ratios

options.text: Pythagorean tuning, where thirds are tuned by thirty-two to twenty-seven.
options.misconception: Confuses Pythagorean third ratios with equal steps

options.text: A meantone tuning, where fifths are narrowed so major thirds come out pure.
options.misconception: Believes meantone fifths produce equal-sized semitones

questions.explanation: Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical semitones, so every step is the same size. The other tunings deliberately distort some intervals, so their step sizes differ.
questions.hint: Equal steps mean equal temperament.

A perfect fourth, because the routine counts the upper note but not the lower one.
options.misconception: Believes the letter count excludes the lower note

options.text: A major sixth, because seven semitones is read as a sixth rather than a fifth.
options.misconception: Believes semitone count alone determines the number

options.text: An augmented fourth, because a fifth of seven semitones is automatically a tritone.
options.misconception: Believes seven semitones always means an augmented fourth

questions.explanation: Counting E, F, G, A and B inclusively gives five letters, and seven semitones is a perfect fifth. Excluding the lower note or using the semitone count as the number both misread the trace.
questions.hint: Count letters inclusively, then check semitones.

questions.topic: What an inversion does to quality and number
questions.learningObjective: Predict how inversion changes interval number and quality
questions.stem: In an engineer's brief, a note pair is inverted by moving the lower note up an octave so the roles of lower and upper swap. Explain how inversion changes an interval's number and quality.

answer.exemplar: Inverting an interval flips which note is lower, so the interval number is replaced by nine minus the original, turning a third into a sixth and a fifth into a fourth. Perfect qualities stay perfect, major becomes minor, minor becomes major, and augmented becomes diminished, because the same two pitches keep the same semitone distance.

questions.explanation: Inversion keeps the same pitches, so the semitone distance stays the same while the letter count becomes nine minus the original. Quality flips too, so perfect stays perfect and major trades with minor.
questions.hint: Number becomes nine minus the original.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Whole step and half step in equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: Justify equal temperament and state its cost
questions.stem: In an engineer's brief, a tuning system must be justified as equal temperament. Explain what makes a temperament equal and what it costs in tuning accuracy.

answer.exemplar: Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical semitones, so every whole step is exactly twice every half step and any key can be tuned the same way. The cost is that pure intervals are slightly distorted: the major third of five to four comes out about 13.7 cents wide, the fifth of three to two about 1.95 cents narrow, and no key is perfectly in tune.

questions.explanation: Equidistant semitones let any note serve as a tonic and make every key equally usable. The price is that intervals pure in just intonation, such as the major third and fifth, come out slightly off.
questions.hint: Equal steps, slightly impure thirds.

options.text: A diminished fifth, since a perfect fifth of seven semitones has been narrowed by one.
An augmented fifth, since six semitones exceeds the perfect fifth of seven.
options.misconception: Treats a smaller count as a wider interval

options.text: A perfect fourth, since six semitones equals one and a half whole steps.
options.misconception: Ignores the letter count when naming the interval

options.text: A minor sixth, since six semitones is the size of a minor sixth.
options.misconception: Confuses the tritone with the minor sixth

answer.exemplar: Equal temperament measures the octave as twelve identical semitones, and a semitone is the smallest step the system recognises. A step that sounds like the distance from one white key to the next, skipping a black key, must therefore cover two of those half steps. questions.explanation: Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal semitones, and the whole step is the larger of the two standard steps, so it measures two of them. The octave itself is then six whole steps.

questions.learningObjective: Derive the size of an octave from the whole step
questions.stem: A tuning log records a system in which the whole step measures 200 cents. How many cents does the octave measure in that system?

options.text: 1200 cents, because an octave spans six whole steps of 200 cents.
1400 cents, because seven whole steps fit into an octave.
options.misconception: Counts seven whole steps in the octave

options.text: 1000 cents, because an octave is five whole steps.
options.misconception: Counts five whole steps in the octave

options.text: 200 cents, because the octave equals one whole step.
options.misconception: Believes the octave is a single whole step

questions.explanation: An octave contains six whole steps, so six times 200 cents gives 1200 cents, the usual size of an octave. Counting seven or five whole steps contradicts the span of the octave.
questions.hint: Six whole steps make an octave.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Naming an interval by number and quality
questions.learningObjective: Trace a quality lookup for a measured interval distance
questions.stem: A routine measures the semitone distance between two notes and matches it to a reference table of interval qualities. Tracing it for a distance of ten semitones, which name does it output?

options.text: A minor seventh, since ten semitones is the reference size for a seventh.
A major seventh, since ten semitones is the reference size for a seventh.
options.misconception: Confuses the minor seventh with the major seventh

options.text: A minor sixth, since ten semitones is the reference size for a sixth.
options.misconception: Assigns the count to the wrong interval number

options.text: A diminished octave, since ten semitones is one short of a full octave.
options.misconception: Treats a near-octave as a diminished octave

questions.explanation: Ten semitones is the reference size of a minor seventh, while a major seventh is eleven semitones. The routine reads quality from the measured distance, so it cannot return a sixth or a diminished octave.
questions.hint: Ten semitones is one short of the eleventh.
